Encapsulating locators and actions into reusable, maintainable classes

BEGINNER1. Why Page Objects Exist

Without a page object, every test that interacts with the login form repeats the same locators and steps:

// Repeated in test after test after test...
await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email);
await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(password);
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

The moment the button label changes from "Sign in" to "Log in," every one of those tests breaks — and you have to fix the same line in dozens of places. The Page Object Model (POM) solves this by encapsulating a page's locators and interactions into one reusable class.

The payoff: when the UI changes, you fix one class, and every test using it is automatically correct again. Tests become short and readable — they describe what the user does, not how the DOM is structured.

BEGINNER2. Anatomy of a Page Object Class

A page object has three parts:

  • A constructor that receives page (and optionally context or request)
  • Locator properties, declared readonly, using page.getByRole(…) etc. — lazy, so they always reflect the current DOM
  • Action methods that group related interactions into meaningful steps
// pages/LoginPage.ts
import { type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export class LoginPage {
  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {}

  readonly emailInput    = this.page.getByLabel('Email');
  readonly passwordInput = this.page.getByLabel('Password');
  readonly submitButton  = this.page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' });
  readonly errorMessage  = this.page.getByRole('alert');

  async goto() {
    await this.page.goto('/login');
  }

  async signIn(email: string, password: string) {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
    await this.passwordInput.fill(password);
    await this.submitButton.click();
  }
}
💡 Tip: Locator properties are re-evaluated every time they're accessed — declaring them once in the constructor's field initializers is safe even before page.goto() has run, because nothing actually queries the DOM until an action or assertion uses the locator.

BEGINNER3. The Golden Rule: Actions in PO, Assertions in Test

Page objects are action libraries, not validators. Keep expect() calls in the test file, not inside the page object class.

❌ Assertion inside the page object: 
async signIn(email, password) {
  await this.emailInput.fill(email);
  await this.submitButton.click();
  // Don't do this here:
  await expect(this.page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
}
✅ Assertion stays in the test: 
await loginPage.signIn(email, password);
await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');

Mixing assertions into page objects makes them harder to reuse (what if one test needs to verify a failed login instead?) and harder to debug (the failure now points into a shared class instead of the specific test).

INTERMEDIATE4. Integrating Page Objects with Fixtures

// fixtures/pages.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage';

export const test = base.extend<{ loginPage: LoginPage }>({
  loginPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(new LoginPage(page));
  },
});

// Usage in tests
import { test, expect } from './fixtures/pages';

test('valid login navigates to dashboard', async ({ loginPage, page }) => {
  await loginPage.goto();
  await loginPage.signIn('user@example.com', 'secret');
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
});

This is the recommended pattern — tests request a page object by name, exactly like requesting page itself, and never have to write new LoginPage(page) repeatedly.

INTERMEDIATE5. Component Objects for Shared UI

For UI elements that appear on many pages — a header, a modal, a data table — create a smaller component object and compose it into whichever page objects use it.

// components/Header.ts
export class Header {
  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {}
  readonly userMenu   = this.page.getByTestId('user-menu');
  readonly signOutBtn = this.page.getByRole('menuitem', { name: 'Sign out' });

  async signOut() {
    await this.userMenu.click();
    await this.signOutBtn.click();
  }
}

// pages/DashboardPage.ts
import { Header } from '../components/Header';

export class DashboardPage {
  readonly header = new Header(this.page);   // composition
  constructor(private readonly page: Page) {}
  async goto() { await this.page.goto('/dashboard'); }
}
Real-world payoff: a Header component object is reused across DashboardPage, ProfilePage, and SettingsPage without duplicating its locators or sign-out logic three times.

ADVANCED6. Composing Multiple Page Objects

// fixtures/pages.ts
type PageObjects = {
  loginPage:     LoginPage;
  dashboardPage: DashboardPage;
  checkoutPage:  CheckoutPage;
};

export const test = base.extend({
  loginPage:     async ({ page }, use) => use(new LoginPage(page)),
  dashboardPage: async ({ page }, use) => use(new DashboardPage(page)),
  checkoutPage:  async ({ page }, use) => use(new CheckoutPage(page)),
});

test('complete purchase flow', async ({ loginPage, dashboardPage, checkoutPage, page }) => {
  await loginPage.goto();
  await loginPage.signIn('user@example.com', 'secret');
  await dashboardPage.addItemToCart('Widget Pro');
  await checkoutPage.completePayment({ card: '4111111111111111' });
  await expect(page).toHaveURL('/confirmation');
});

Long end-to-end journeys become readable as a sequence of page-object method calls, each one expressing intent rather than DOM mechanics.

ADVANCED7. Page Objects vs Raw Locators — When to Bother

Situation Recommendation
Small suite, few pages, short-lived project Raw locators inline may be simpler — POM adds overhead you might not need yet
Multiple tests reuse the same flow (login, navigation) Extract a page object — the duplication cost already outweighs the setup cost
Large, growing suite maintained by a team POM strongly recommended — the maintainability payoff compounds over time

ADVANCED8. Common Pitfalls

⚠️ Pitfall 1 — "God" page objects: Cramming every locator and action for an entire application into one giant class defeats the purpose. Split by page or feature, and use component objects for anything shared.
⚠️ Pitfall 2 — Storing locators as plain fields evaluated once: Declaring this.emailInput = this.page.locator(...) is fine (locators are lazy), but caching the result of calling an action too early — e.g. storing a resolved element handle from before navigation — reintroduces the stale-element problems locators were designed to avoid. Stick to Locator objects, never elementHandle(), in page objects.

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
Structure Constructor(page) + readonly locator properties + async action methods.
Golden rule Actions in the page object; assertions stay in the test.
Fixture integration Wrap `new PageObject(page)` in a test.extend() fixture for clean test signatures.
Component objects Extract shared UI (header, modal, table) and compose into full page objects.
When to use POM Worth it once a flow (like login) is reused across more than a couple of tests.
